summary: Brief observation of a shape of the same size, intensity, color as the Moon very close: probable observation of paraselene.
description: Recent report (June 2014) of an old observation. On December 5, 2003, between 8:00 and 8:30 PM, a witness telephoned a friend who was standing by the window when he observed a motionless, white, oval shape in the sky. This shape was very close to the Moon, almost identical in size, and of the same color and intensity. The glow disappeared quickly. The observation lasted between 15 and 20 seconds. Only one report has been collected about this phenomenon. Due to its strangeness and lack of consistency (short observation of 20 seconds, single witness, no photograph, late report, inconsistency between the reported and actual position of the Moon, atmospheric conditions), this case is a probable observation of an atmospheric optical phenomenon called a paraselene (see the investigation notes). It should also be noted that the late testimony, nearly 10 years after the events, certainly led to memory errors (sky, stars, and the position of the Moon). This case is class B, probable observation of a paraselene.
On December 3, 2003, the crew of a Boeing 737 reported a very brief luminous phenomenon crossing the atmosphere, probably caused by atmospheric reentry.

summary: Observation of the presence and silent movement of two dark objects: trajectory mainly straight but with abrupt changes of direction. Lack of information.
description: Recent report (October 3, 2012) of an old sighting, the date of which remains approximate according to the witness. On September 15, 2003, around 9:30 PM, a person observed the successive appearance in the sky of two dark, triangular objects equipped with several lights. Initially stationary, then moving rapidly with changes of direction, they disappeared towards sunset. No sound was heard during the observation. The witness illustrated their account with a photo of the 1990 Petit-Rechain case in Belgium, specifying that there was more brightness during their observation. Due to the variable light located in the middle of the triangle, it could be a case of mistaken identity with an airplane or helicopter, observed from a distance sufficient to avoid being heard. The imprecision regarding the date and the age of the observation make a serious investigation impossible. This case is classified as "C" due to lack of information.

summary: Observation of 2 fixed points high in the sky, which then moved very quickly and disappeared after a few seconds.
description: On August 19, 2003, at approximately 11:40 PM, two fixed points high in the sky were observed. They then moved very rapidly and disappeared after a few seconds. Information about this observation is very limited, hence its classification as C.

summary: Observation of flashing lights passing across the sky, resembling a large aircraft.
description: On August 9, 2003, at approximately 11:00 PM, a witness and their family observed flashing lights in the sky, resembling a large aircraft. Due to insufficient information, this was classified as a Class C phenomenon.

summary: Observation of flashes of white color.
description: Direct testimony: Sometime in August 2003 (the witness no longer remembers the exact day), around midnight, five people gathered in the village square to observe the stars witnessed a peculiar luminous phenomenon. While looking at the sky and observing shooting stars, they were "flashed" for half a second by two rows of three spotlights directly above them. The flash was white, the intensity of the light was significant, and it illuminated the area as brightly as daylight. The spotlights gradually went out over the course of a second. The entire event occurred without any sound. No other accounts have been collected regarding this phenomenon, about which we lack information.

On February 22, 2003, at approximately 7:10 AM, a witness observed the very rapid passage of a luminous red-orange sphere with a trail. The phenomenon, which lasted only a few seconds, was likely an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Observation of the passage of a group of luminous spheres coming from Belgium: lack of information.
description: witness reported in August 2009 an observation made in July 2003. Around 2 PM, several people in a garden observed the silent passage of twenty to thirty orbs across the blue sky. These orbs came from the northeast and were heading southwest. The observation lasted approximately 10 minutes. Only one witness account was collected. This account was deemed unusable by GEIPAN (the French National Group for the Study of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena). Indeed, it was given six years after the observation and did not specify the date (July 2003... that's all). The description is not particularly strange, as it is consistent with the release of balloons. Without a date, there is no way to confirm the hypothesis regarding the wind direction. GEIPAN classifies the report as C: Lack of information.

summary: Multiple observations by pilots of an intense but brief luminous phenomenon: probable atmospheric reentry.
description: On June 11, 2003, at approximately 2:30 AM, the crews of several aircraft observed for a few seconds the passage of a strong blue-green glow that appeared very close to the aircraft for some crew members. This glow was probably due to atmospheric reentry.

On April 7, 2003, around midnight, a witness observed the brief passage of a green light, the size of a very large star, falling vertically and disappearing before hitting the ground. This was likely an atmospheric reentry.

Periodic observations of light sources, beams of light illuminating the witness's house, and several "landings" were reported. All investigations conducted failed to corroborate the witness's statements, and no trace of anything was found at the alleged landing sites. The behavior of any other potential witnesses, as well as that of his wife, casts doubt on the credibility of this testimony.

summary: Plausible observations of an atmospheric reentry.
description: On March 21, 2003, at approximately 8:15 PM, several people in the Aude and Landes regions witnessed the very rapid and silent fall of a greenish ball. As it was likely an atmospheric reentry, the observation was classified as category B.

summary: Observation by several witnesses of the fall which caused an impact on the ground
description: On March 3, 2004, at approximately 4:00 PM, several witnesses observed an object falling. The object made an impact on the ground, which was felt by the witnesses and recorded by the Institute of Earth Physics in Strasbourg. Aerial maneuvers involving several helicopters were taking place in the area at the time of the observation. The sighting was classified as Category B, which could be explained by a meteorite impact or a ground impact related to the aerial maneuvers.

summary: Observation of triangular points during the examination of photographs
description: After transferring the photographs to his computer, the witness noticed a triangle appearing in one of the pictures. Lacking precise information, the phenomenon is classified as Class C.

summary: Observation of a large triangular object with 9 orange rings
description: On February 5, 2003, at approximately 6:50 PM, a witness observed a large triangular object with nine orange rings. The object emitted a faint whirring sound, similar to an airplane. The weather was cloudy. After remaining stationary for a few seconds, the object rotated 45 degrees, began an upward trajectory, and then disappeared. This unexplained phenomenon was classified as Class D.

summary: Observation of the very rapid and silent passage of a fluorescent green luminous phenomenon in the sky: probable observation of a meteoroid reentry.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named CORTE (2B) 2003, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On Saturday, January 11, 2003, around 6:15-6:20 PM, a driver and passenger traveling on the RN193 towards Corte (2B) were surprised by the rapid and silent passage of a bright green light with white flashes across the sky. Witnesses describe a circular shape. During the observation, which lasted a few seconds, the object moved along a south-north trajectory. The witnesses' description, under a clear night sky, is typical of an atmospheric reentry observation of a meteoroid: short duration of a few seconds, high angular velocity; multiple intense colors: green (fluorescent), yellow, with halos. Here, the witnesses do not describe trails but rather a round shape. Witness T1 distinguishes various internal details within this circle, such as openings and position lights. Witness T2 notes no details within this luminous circle, which he also describes at the end as a "streak of light." There is no perception of noise, but the witnesses are in a car, and a meteoroid is often silent to witnesses. Since 2003, the date of the observation, GEIPAN's experience with this type of sighting has greatly increased, also through collaboration with specialized sighting collection sites (IMO, BOAM, FRIPON, REFORME). Given the descriptive elements frequently present in confirmed meteoroid re-entries (observed with numerous overlapping observations over large distances on the ground, thanks also to the aforementioned sites), there is a strong probability that this observation is also a meteoroid re-entry. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable meteoroid re-entry observation.
